questions.q: Why does this lesson say a consistent naming convention matters, beyond tidiness?
options: Salesforce requires unique prefixes on every automation or it won't save
It lets the next person understand what an automation does without opening it, and renaming later touches every reference to it
It increases an org's storage limits
It is required for validation rules to run in order
questions.explain: A rule named for its object, purpose, and condition is self-documenting at a glance, and picking the convention early avoids a costly rename later.

questions.q: What does the Description field on a validation rule or approval process ideally capture?
options: A restatement of the formula itself
The business reason it exists, any non-obvious edge case, and what would break if it were removed
The name of the Salesforce release it was created in
A list of every user who can view the object
questions.explain: The formula already shows what the rule checks. The Description should capture the why, which is what's lost when someone else has to maintain it later.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend deactivating automation before deleting it?
options: Deactivating is required before Salesforce allows any edits
Deactivated automation is still present and restorable in seconds, while deletion is permanent and destroys configuration history
Deleted automation can be restored from the Recycle Bin indefinitely
Deactivation automatically documents the change for you
questions.explain: Deactivating is reversible and gives you a safety window to confirm nothing depended on the automation silently, before committing to permanent deletion.

questions.q: Which of these is a sign it may be time to consolidate automation on an object?
options: The object has exactly one validation rule
Two or more rules or flows read or write the same field, and new admins keep asking why several rules do almost the same thing
The object has no automation at all
A Flow was deactivated six months ago
questions.explain: Overlapping writes to the same field and repeated confusion from new admins are concrete signals that automation has accumulated past the point of easy maintenance.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against treating consolidation as a "free cleanup"?
options: Because consolidation is itself a change to production automation and needs sandbox testing like any other change
Because Salesforce charges extra for consolidating automation
Because consolidated rules can never be deactivated afterward
Because consolidation always requires writing Apex
questions.explain: It's easy to assume cleanup is low-risk because nothing new is being added, but combining existing logic can change behavior in subtle ways, so it deserves the same testing discipline as a new feature.
